assessment_summary: The proof relies on classifying subgroups of S_7 generated by two 7-cycles in Case 1. The classification provided in step 0025 explicitly states that these subgroups must be C_7, PSL(2,7), or S_7. However, this claim is mathematically false. Since 7-cycles are even permutations, they can only generate subgroups of the alternating group A_7, so they can never generate S_7. Furthermore, they can generate A_7, which is missing from the author's list. A concrete counterexample is provided showing two 7-cycles that generate A_7.
counterexample:
The claim in step 0025 that "every subgroup of S_7 generated by two 7-cycles is either a cyclic group of order 7, the group PSL(2,7) we want, or all of S_7" is false. Since a 7-cycle is an even permutation, two 7-cycles can only generate subgroups of the alternating group A_7, making S_7 impossible. Furthermore, they can generate A_7, which is omitted from the list. 

As a concrete counterexample, let \sigma = (1,2,3,4,5,6,7) and \tau = (1,2,3,4,5,7,6). The permutation \sigma^{-1}\tau evaluates to the single 3-cycle (5,6,7). Conjugating this 3-cycle by \sigma repeatedly yields the 3-cycles (6,7,1), (7,1,2), (1,2,3), (2,3,4), (3,4,5), and (4,5,6). It is a standard result that these 3-cycles generate the full alternating group A_7. Thus, \langle \sigma, \tau \rangle = A_7, which is a subgroup generated by two 7-cycles that is not C_7, PSL(2,7), or S_7.
